content:
I have recently opened a PR porting the language interface in program_logic/language.v to Lean. I made some changes to the definitions, some out of necessity (there are no canonical structures in Lean), some out of convenience, some to make them more idiomatic. Because of this, I wanted to ask for some feedback on some of these changes.

Typeclasses instead of canonical structures

I had to make some decissions on how to restructure the language definition so they would make more sense in Lean. In particular, I translated the language structure into the Language typeclass. In the end I marked State, Val and Obs as outParams in my definition, so they are all linked to a single concreteExpr type. Originally I didn't want to make this change, which is why the Language typeclass is defined by extending two other typeclasses, PrimStep and ToVal, which was my initial attempt at a solution (this allowed me to define reducible and others without having to specify Val).

I would like feedback on this design choice, in particular

  • Does it make sense to assume Expr is the only non-outParam in the typeclass?
  • Does it make sense to keep ToVal and PrimStep as separate typeclasses, or should I just directly embed them into Language?

Custom notation

While working on translating the file, I thought it would be useful to have some notation for the different kinds of steps that can be found. My motivation was to improve readability. This is something which is explicitly not done in the Rocq version, and I was wondering whether it would be ok to leave it here or if I should do away with it.

Uncurried primStep signature :warning:

When defining the custom notations, I decided to have primStep defined as a relation on pairs Expr × State. I have since been warned that this could be potentially dangerous, and wanted to get some input on whether it makes sense to have or not.

Making ofVal an implicit coercion

I also made the decision to create a Coe Val Expr instance out of ofVal, to improve the readability of some lemmas. It also helps hide the fact that ofVal is not able to infer the type of Expr, so one has to write (v : Expr) to call ofVal instead of ofVal (Expr := Expr) v.

For 1, I think that makes sense. I wouldn't expect more than one language instance for any Expr syntax in scope at once. Also: adding notation is generally fine.

For the others, I have no thoughts, if I were you I'd just try it out and see what works. Maybe other people have more knowledge thought.

It is great to see that you are making fast progress on this! My thoughts on your questions:

In general, I would recommend that you use Exp instead of Expr. Expr is already used for the type of Lean terms used in meta programming and having two different Expr can be quite confusing.

Does it make sense to assume Expr is the only non-outParam in the typeclass?

At first glance this seems sensible to me, but one would need to try how well it works in practice.

(there are no canonical structures in Lean),

This is not exactly true. You can achieve the effect of canonical structures in Lean by using unif_hint. However, I am not sure how recommended it is to use unif_hint (it is not even documented in the Lean reference). So it might be better to first try if one can make it work with typeclasses. The problem that typeclasses cause in Rocq (exponential blowup) should not be a problem in Lean since Lean is better at sharing subterms.

Does it make sense to keep ToVal and PrimStep as separate typeclasses, or should I just directly embed them into Language?

Do you have use cases where you would actually want to use them on their own? If yes, splitting them up would make sense. If not, it might be easier to just merge them into the Language typeclass. This might also be something to try out.

While working on translating the file, I thought it would be useful to have some notation for the different kinds of steps that can be found.

Which notations are these? I have not strong opinion on this, my rule of thumb would be the question how useful these notations would be to clients. If the notations are only used in a single file, I am not sure if it makes sense to have them.

When defining the custom notations, I decided to have primStep defined as a relation on pairs Expr × State. I have since been warned that this could be potentially dangerous, and wanted to get some input on whether it makes sense to have or not.

This would be something to try out I guess.

I also made the decision to create a Coe Val Expr instance out of ofVal, to improve the readability of some lemmas.

I personally have not had good experience with coercions in Lean. They sometimes don't fire when I expect them to fire. But this might also just be me not understanding them. I guess this is also something to try out.

In summary, things to try out:

  1. Whether to keep ToVal and PrimStep as separate classes
  2. Steps being defined as relations on pairs.
  3. Whether the Coe Val Expr makes sense or not

Regarding (1), I'm already seeing some arguments in favor of keeping them when working on ectx_language. In particular, an ectx_language also requires a notion of to_val and of_val, for which I can just embed the ToVal typeclass directly, and reuse previous lemmas.

About (3), to be fair I wasn't thinking about using coercions as a way to sneakily convert Val to Expr, but to enable using type ascription to invoke ofVal, so I am not too worried about them not firing when I expect them to. I'm more worried about them triggering when we don't want them to, but I can't imagine many contexts in which they'd do. I have heard of horror stories with regards to coercions though, so it might be best to play it by ear.

Michael Sammler said:

Which notations are these?

I have added tests for the notations I defined, so you can find a collection of all of them here. Feel free to judge me on my aesthetic sense! (also, some of these work better with a font with ligatures, like mine)

I also haven't had the chance to see whether they'll be useful in more than one file or not, but I expect that to change in the coming days as I move forward with the port

Michael Sammler said:

In general, I would recommend that you use Exp instead of Expr. Expr is already used for the type of Lean terms used in meta programming and having two different Expr can be quite confusing.

I'm not a big fan of Exp, to me it reads as "experience" and not really "expression". I wouldn't mind chaning it if people think it's an issue though, I won't die on this hill. I just don't see there being many opportunities for confusion, since it's just a type variable, and it doesn't make it to definitions (like, there is not a toExpr function or similar, which could get confusing with Lean.ToExpr), but I see the argument if at some point these sort of functions were to be needed.

Fernando LEAL said:

but to enable using type ascription to invoke ofVal

Maybe one can get rid of these type ascriptions by changing what are input and outputs to ToVal? Maybe there Val should be an input and Expr an outParam? Or maybe both Val and Expr should be semiOutParam? (Not sure if any of these ideas work, but might be worth playing around a bit with the typeclasses to see if one can find something works and does not need type ascriptions.)

Fernando LEAL said:

I just don't see there being many opportunities for confusion, since it's just a type variable, and it doesn't make it to definitions

I would expect that when you define a concrete language like HeapLang, you would name the type of expressions the same as the meta type variable, i.e. Expr. (This is at least how it works in Rocq.) And then when you write a meta program about these expressions (e.g. the wp_load tactic), you have two Expr that one is working with (the Lean Expr and the HeapLang Expr), which will be very confusing. So I think it is just clearer if we use something different than Expr for expressions of our languages. Exp is only one suggestion, I am fine with other names as well as long as they are not Expr.

Michael Sammler said:

Maybe one can get rid of these type ascriptions by changing what are input and outputs to ToVal? Maybe there Val should be an input and Expr an outParam? Or maybe both Val and Expr should be semiOutParam? (Not sure if any of these ideas work, but might be worth playing around a bit with the typeclasses to see if one can find something works and does not need type ascriptions.)

I played around a bit with these definitions, and I arrived to the conclussion that what I have is what works best. It seems natural to infer Val from Expr, since Expr is the common type that relates all others (State and Val, for instance), and making them semiOutParams doesn't seem to fix the issue of having to give explicitly one or the other.

Michael Sammler said:

I would expect that when you define a concrete language like HeapLang, you would name the type of expressions the same as the meta type variable, i.e. Expr. (This is at least how it works in Rocq.) And then when you write a meta program about these expressions (e.g. the wp_load tactic), you have two Expr that one is working with (the Lean Expr and the HeapLang Expr), which will be very confusing. So I think it is just clearer if we use something different than Expr for expressions of our languages. Exp is only one suggestion, I am fine with other names as well as long as they are not Expr.

I'm still not convinced, I don't see how having Expr vs Exp makes much of a difference when distinguishing with Lean.Expr, that isn't also achieved by giving the namespace name directly to disambiguate. I think at a glace one wouldn't even notice the difference, and it would only become evident when someone mistakenly adds the r when writting names down. It seems like you are talking from experience though. If that's so, I will just defer to your expertise. If we don't want Expr I gues Exp is the next best thing.

I have also recently pushed the next PR which also includes EctxLanguage and EctxiLanguage. I think the PR is pretty much done, the only things I would like to revisit are maybe the names of some of the theorems, since I'm not sure how to name them so they can be easily searchable / they follow Mathlib naming guidelines. For those I have simply left the Rocq name for now.

It also has become a quite big PR, at 1400 LoC, so I was wondering whether maybe splitting into three PRs. The reason I haven't done so yet is because I feel like comments for changes to Language.lean would also apply to EctxLanguage.lean and EctxiLanguage.lean, so maybe it makes sense to keep them together.

Fernando LEAL said:

I'm still not convinced, I don't see how having Expr vs Exp makes much of a difference when distinguishing with Lean.Expr, that isn't also achieved by giving the namespace name directly to disambiguate.

The problem is that usually the namespace is not explicitly used. So if I have a function def f (e : Expr) I would now need to see which namespaces are open to figure out if it is Lean.Expr or HeapLang.Expr. If they have different names, it would be def f (e : Exp) or def f (e : Expr) and it would be clear immediately.

Michael Sammler said:

it would be clear immediately.

... if you happen to remember this entirely non-obvious convention ;)
what do other developments that involve an "expression" type usually do in lean?

seems a bit sad to me to have a namespace system and then still use globally unique names even when that is clearly awkward. I mean, we do that in rocq because the module system there is terrible, but I was hoping that in lean we wouldn't have to do this^^

ralfj said:

... if you happen to remember this entirely non-obvious convention ;)

Well, I think if one works with the Exp type for a bit in Lean, one will remember that it is called Exp. But this is also why I think it is important to have this discussion now. We can now decide that the convention for expression types in Iris Lean is Exp, Expr, or something else. Once the convention is established, people working with Iris Lean will learn it. So I think by we should discuss this carefully now, such that we can avoid confusion down the road.

ralfj said:

what do other developments that involve an "expression" type usually do in lean?

I am not sure. CSLib seems to use Term for expressions of the lambda calculus.

ralfj said:

seems a bit sad to me to have a namespace system and then still use globally unique names even when that is clearly awkward. I mean, we do that in rocq because the module system there is terrible, but I was hoping that in lean we wouldn't have to do this^^

I am not sure of how much use the namespace system is in this concrete case since the Lean.Expr type is in the very generic Lean namespace and one often does open Lean, making Expr a top-level name. I guess we could consistently use HeapLang.Expr and don't open the HeapLang namespace, but this might become a bit unwieldy. (Maybe this is preferable to Exp?)

Michael Sammler said:

Fernando LEAL said:

I'm still not convinced, I don't see how having Expr vs Exp makes much of a difference when distinguishing with Lean.Expr, that isn't also achieved by giving the namespace name directly to disambiguate.

The problem is that usually the namespace is not explicitly used. So if I have a function def f (e : Expr)

You could just hover over Expr.
The editor will tell you which Expr you are using
As for open Lean I am unsure about recommended practices but I usually put such code in a section or use the open Lean in <declaration> style.

ralfj said:

what do other developments that involve an "expression" type usually do in lean?

I found an example which uses Expr, but it has a much smaller scope. It is only referenced in Lean/Meta/Tactic/Simp/Arith/Nat/Basic.lean other than in the file where it's defined, and there it's reexported as LinearExpr.

Michael Sammler said:

I am not sure of how much use the namespace system is in this concrete case since the Lean.Expr type is in the very generic Lean namespace and one often does open Lean, making Expr a top-level name

But if one wants to be carefull about which expression they're talking about, they can still reference it as Lean.Expr, even if the Lean namespace has been opened. And in any case, you can't reference both Lean.Expr and HeapLang.Expr both as Expr in a function, so when both are encountered in the same function, there'll need to be disambiguation in any case. Maybe we could make it a convention to always add the namespace around the Lean.Expr expressions.

I agree with these arguments that one can make using Expr work, i.e. why using Expr is not a bad decision. However, I think it would also be good to have arguments why using Expr is actually a good decision, i.e. what the benefits it gives are. Is it just because people are used to Expr and Exp looks weird? Or is there some other advantage?

(For me personally, Expr and Exp seem a priori both fine, but Expr has the downside of the name clash, so for me Exp seems preferable. Based on the discussion I think one can also make Expr work, but that does not seem like an argument in favor of it, it only weakens arguments against it.)

Fair point. The original reason I chose to use Expr is for consistency. Expressions are a concept that is already present in Lean, through its metaprogramming capabilities, and there they made a choice to refer to them as Expr. I was simply mimicking that choice.

The advantage of consistency is that it aids in discoverability, users of the library don't have to guess what the name is, since they can just assume it'll be the most "idiomatic" choice for the platform.

Later it has occured to me that having Expr and Exp be two different concepts accesible under the same namespace may lead to problems, by people making typos and using Expr when they meant Exp or viceversa. Not huge problems, but I could imagine myself finding it annoying. If both are named Expr, Lean will force you to disambiguate, since you can't refer to them both under the same name.

To address the issue of greping for Expr in the codebase showing you instances of different Expr types, we could enforce a convention saying that Lean.Expr should always we refered to as such. Maybe even implement a linter to enforce this rule, such as those found in Mathlib.

It is true that if I do open Lean and open HeapLang, I won't be able to refer to either of those with Expr, since Lean will force you to be explicit about the namespaces for both instances. But in those cases, we can just do open Lean hiding Expr or open Lean renaming Expr → LeanExpr.

Fernando LEAL said:

The original reason I chose to use Expr is for consistency. Expressions are a concept that is already present in Lean, through its metaprogramming capabilities, and there they made a choice to refer to them as Expr. I was simply mimicking that choice.

This is an interesting point, because I actually see it the opposite way. For me, Lean.Expr and HeapLang.Expr are two very different things and for me it is inconsistent for them to have the same name. Lean.Expr is a meta-level concept of the prover while HeapLang.Expr is an object level concept of a concrete language that is modeled.

Fernando LEAL said:

It is true that if I do open Lean and open HeapLang, I won't be able to refer to either of those with Expr, since Lean will force you to be explicit about the namespaces for both instances. But in those cases, we can just do open Lean hiding Expr or open Lean renaming Expr → LeanExpr.

I was not fully aware how these conflicts are handled in Lean, but this is actually quite nice.
Given that we have discussed this question quite a bit now, I think it makes sense to ask what other people think about this.

/poll What should the convention for the name of the expression type in Iris Lean be?
Exp
Expr

Michael Sammler said:

For me, Lean.Expr and HeapLang.Expr are two very different things and for me it is inconsistent for them to have the same name. Lean.Expr is a meta-level concept of the prover while HeapLang.Expr is an object level concept of a concrete language that is modeled.

Fair point. I still see it as them being the same concept, just applied to different levels of abstraction. I do agree that it's dangerous to confuse them, but (1) I think this is a problem that can be properly addressed within the tools given by Lean today and (2) I don't like Exp as the alternative definition, since it's too similar to Expr, and I believe could actually cause more confusion (maybe it's just me who recognizes words through not much more than the first two letters). If we were to decide to really differentiate Lean.Expr from other types of expressions, I think I would be happier with a more different name such as Term (which I'm also not super happy with, my best solution in this regard would be to rename Lean.Expr to MetaExpr and leave Expr for our usecase, but I don't believe it to be whithin scope)
I think "term" is not great, that moves us quite far away fro standard iris practice (both in Rocq and on paper)
these things are consistently called "expressions"

that can reasonably be abbreviated as Expr or Exp, though Expr is more common.
I think disambiguating Lean expressions from HeapLang expressiosn via a trailing "r" is a bad choice since it is non-self-explaining: when I read code and see "HeapLang.Expr"/"Lean.Expr", I can tell what that means. When I see "Exp" and "Expr" I am likely to miss the difference, and even when I notice it I have to do some research to figure out what the trailing "r" is supposed to tell me.

Michael Sammler said:

For me, Lean.Expr and HeapLang.Expr are two very different things and for me it is inconsistent for them to have the same name. Lean.Expr is a meta-level concept of the prover while HeapLang.Expr is an object level concept of a concrete language that is modeled.

"Exp" is still short for "expression", so apparently you agree that both of these are, conceptually, expressions. I dont see how presence or lack of a trailing r is a useful indicator for "meta-level concept in prover" vs "object-level concept of language". In contrast, Lean.Expr vs HeapLang.Expr indicates that difference very well.

In LeanMLIR, we just called our object language expressions Expr and did not use open Lean, but rather used Lean.Expr explicitly when writing metacode using both types of expressions (e.g. in https://github.com/opencompl/lean-mlir/blob/77fa1c1507a61369f6d9a8ab3de54b9bbe5e1393/LeanMLIR/LeanMLIR/Framework/ToExpr.lean#L103)

To me, Exp vs Expr feels like a footgun that will be very hard to remember, whereas giving them the same (namespaced) name encourages not blindly opening the Lean namespace, and Expr vs Lean.Expr is much more obvious.

Alex Keizer said:

In LeanMLIR, we just called our object language expressions Expr and did not use open Lean, but rather used Lean.Expr explicitly when writing metacode using both types of expressions (e.g. in https://github.com/opencompl/lean-mlir/blob/77fa1c1507a61369f6d9a8ab3de54b9bbe5e1393/LeanMLIR/LeanMLIR/Framework/ToExpr.lean#L103)

To me, Exp vs Expr feels like a footgun that will be very hard to remember, whereas giving them the same (namespaced) name encourages not blindly opening the Lean namespace, and Expr vs Lean.Expr is much more obvious.

Thank you for your input. It's nice to have an examlpe that is a bit bigger than the ones I had found before. I didn't know about this project, it looks cool!

This is an interesting point, because I actually see it the opposite way. For me, Lean.Expr and HeapLang.Expr are two very different things and for me it is inconsistent for them to have the same name.

At the risk of continueing the bikeshed: although they serve pretty different functinos, I would still colloqually call both expressions. Again, based on my LeanMLIR experience, when documenting code in prose we would generally refer to the object expressions as just "expression", since that one was used way more often and the LeanMLIR namespace was basically always open, whereas in the few occasions we also talked about Lean's expressions we would disambiguate, in prose, by calling them "Lean expressions".

Exactly because these two things serve pretty different functions, it helps to give them the same name, as it forces you to be explicit about which one you mean, whether it's in prose ("expression" vs "lean expression") or in code (Expr vs Lean.Expr).
Thanks for sharing your experience, Alex! This is a very useful data point. Given all this discussion, I am also happy with Expr instead of Exp.

By the way, I believe my language interface PRs are pretty much finished and so ready for review. Since we got a bit sidetracked with the Expr discussion, I thought I would mention it to get back on track. All comments I made my prior message still apply, althought since then I addressed some feedback provided by Max (idk if they're the @maxv in this Zulip)
@Markus de Medeiros What is your current capacity to review these PRs? I was hoping to find the time to look over the PR, but last week and this week was / is very busy for me.
I will be on vacation until Thursday, at which point I can help review.
